title: Mlai senior domain fairness tradeoffs
question: What does it mean for a model to be fair, and why can't you generally satisfy every definition of fairness at once?
idealAnswer:
There are multiple, mathematically distinct fairness definitions, e.g. demographic parity, equal positive prediction rate across groups, equalized odds, equal true and false positive rates across groups, and predictive parity, equal precision across groups

It's a known theoretical result that, except in special cases, these definitions cannot all be satisfied simultaneously when base rates differ between groups, so choosing a fairness criterion is itself a value judgment, not a purely technical one

Removing a protected attribute, e.g. race, from the model's inputs doesn't guarantee fairness, other correlated features, e.g. zip code, can act as proxies and reintroduce the same bias

Bias can enter from the training data itself if historical outcomes reflect past discrimination, a model trained to predict those outcomes will learn to reproduce that discrimination

A strong answer connects the choice of fairness metric to the actual stakes and context of the decision, e.g. a lending model and a search ranking model may reasonably prioritize different fairness definitions
